name: Tailoring (any clothes)
lead: Tailoring, in the sense used in style and grooming discussions, is the practice of having a tailor alter ready-made clothing so that it follows the wearer's measurements, for example by hemming trousers, taking in a shirt or shortening sleeves. A tailor is a person who makes or alters clothing, particularly men's clothing, and the Oxford English Dictionary dates the English term to the thirteenth century [1]. A more extensive service, called bespoke or made-to-measure, constructs a garment to the individual, whereas alterations are smaller adjustments to existing garments that are generally quicker and cheaper [2][4][6].

Tailoring improves how a person looks by making clothes follow the body: sleeves and trouser hems end where they should, shoulders and waist sit close to the frame, and the garment shows the wearer's proportions rather than hiding or swamping them. Style writers often describe fit as mattering more than brand or price, and altering ready-made clothing is presented as an inexpensive way to change how a physique and outfit read. A 2011 University of Hertfordshire study, carried out with a tailoring firm, found that observers shown a man for three seconds rated him as more confident, successful and higher-earning in a made-to-measure suit than in a similar off-the-peg suit [3].

The craft has a long documented history, including medieval guilds, apprenticeship systems, regional house styles, the Savile Row bespoke tradition in London and the later growth of ready-to-wear clothing, whose standard sizes made alteration a separate everyday service [1][4][5][7].

angle.text: Tailoring changes how clothes sit on the body, so the same physique looks more proportionate in a garment that follows its lines. People use it on ordinary off-the-rack clothes, most often trousers, shirts and jackets.

paras: Alterations modify a finished garment: trouser hems and waistbands, shirt sides and sleeve lengths, and jacket sleeves are common examples. Because the work removes or repositions fabric within the garment's existing seam allowances, how much can be changed depends on how the piece was originally cut [2]. The Wikipedia article on suits notes, for instance, that sleeve length must be settled before working buttonholes are cut because it cannot be altered afterward [8].

Three levels of service are usually distinguished. Ready-to-wear is factory-made in standard sizes. Made-to-measure alters a standard base pattern to the customer's measurements and posture, with fewer fittings than bespoke and often with some machine sewing [6]. Bespoke, or custom, tailoring makes the garment to an individual's specification without a pre-existing pattern [4].

Wikipedia describes a bespoke suit as starting with a consultation on fabric, lining and styling, followed by measurement (often twenty or more measurements), drafting of a new pattern, cutting and loose basting for a first fitting, two to three fittings in total and finishing over a period of typically two to three months [4]. Wikipedia's tailor article adds that even with modern machinery about three quarters of the stitching in a custom suit is still done by hand, and that some cutters draft freehand with chalk, a method called rock of eye [1].

Tailoring traditions are described in terms of regional house styles. The British cut has a defined waist and structured shoulders built with heavier canvassing and fabrics of about 9 to 13 ounces, and is associated with Henry Poole and H. Huntsman and Sons; the Drape cut is credited to Frederick Scholte. The Italian cut is described as lighter and softer, with fabrics of about 7 to 9 ounces and more natural shoulders, with Cesare Attolini credited with the lighter Neapolitan construction. The American cut is described as a blend of the two, roomier with light canvas, and the Ivy League look is its best-known form [1].

Wikipedia reports tailor shops and tools such as shears and irons in ancient Greece and Rome, and a formalised profession in medieval Europe organised through guilds with masters, journeymen and apprentices. In 1244 tailors in Bologna adopted statutes governing their trade, and in England the Statute of Artificers of 1563 listed tailoring among trades entered by apprenticeship, typically of seven years; the statute was repealed in 1814 [1]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, similarly describes tailoring emerging between the twelfth and fourteenth centuries as fashions shifted to fitted garments, and places the London tailors' fraternity in records from about 1300 [2].

Padding men's jackets with underlayers was fashionable in Europe by the fourteenth century, and by the nineteenth century garments were fitted with a more subtle understructure. The earliest surviving treatise on cutting by a tailor is attributed to Juan de Alcega of Spain in 1580, and patterns were treated as trade secrets until about 1790 [1].

In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries the trade became more specialised and, in Britain, a major employer; the 1851 census counted 152,672 tailors, and cheap ready-made clothing known as slops was one factor changing working conditions [1]. Wikipedia notes that standardised sizes appeared in the early 1800s as makers observed that body dimensions fell within a fairly narrow range, making mass production practical, and that sizing systems have since varied by maker and country, including through vanity sizing [7]. Brooks Brothers is generally credited with the first ready-to-wear suit [8]. Off-the-rack sizing that fits an average build is the reason alterations form a market of their own [2][7].

Savile Row in Mayfair, London, was built between 1731 and 1735, tailors began arriving in the late eighteenth century and had reached the street itself by 1803 [5]. Henry Poole and Co opened a Savile Row entrance in 1846 and is credited with the dinner jacket, after making a smoking jacket for the young Edward VII in 1860; H. Huntsman and Sons was founded in 1849 [5]. Per Anderson of Anderson and Sheppard, a protege of Frederick Scholte, developed the London cut, with a high, small armhole and generous upper sleeve [5].

The street also entered popular culture: Nutters of Savile Row, opened in 1969, dressed the Beatles and Mick Jagger, and the Beatles' last live performance took place on the roof of Apple's building at 3 Savile Row on 30 January 1969 [5]. A New Bespoke Movement in the 1990s, led by Richard James, Ozwald Boateng and Timothy Everest, modernised the style, and the Savile Row Bespoke Association was founded in 2004; its members typically put at least 50 hours of hand labour into a two-piece suit [5].

The word bespoke is itself a point of contention. Wikipedia reports that in June 2008 the UK Advertising Standards Authority ruled that describing a machine-assisted suit as bespoke was not misleading, relying on the Oxford English Dictionary's definition of bespoke as made to order, and that critics of the ruling said it blurred the distinction with made-to-measure [4][6].

sections.h: How it is said to work
paras: Proponents describe the mechanism as geometric: when shoulders, waist, sleeve and hem lengths line up with the wearer's body, the garment follows the body's lines rather than hanging loosely or pulling. The Suit article describes tailoring as aiming for a balanced silhouette in which the jacket does not pull or hang loose when unbuttoned [8]. Observers' first impressions are the proposed route from fit to perceived status, as in the Hertfordshire study below.
No published study located for this article has measured whether altering an off-the-rack garment changes ratings of attractiveness or status.

The best-documented research is the 2011 Hertfordshire study led by Karen Pine and Ben Fletcher, in which more than 300 participants aged 14 to 67 viewed pictures with the faces blanked out and judged each person within three seconds. The man in a made-to-measure suit was rated as more confident, successful and flexible, and as earning more, than the same man in a similar off-the-peg suit [3]. The study was run in collaboration with Mathieson and Brooke Tailors, and the report noted it had not yet been peer reviewed [3]. Pine was quoted saying the study endorsed with real evidence that people form opinions quickly [3].
Laura Ugolini's 2003 study, cited by Wikipedia, found that well-informed male consumers generally preferred bespoke suits, which they saw as better quality and value [4].

Style writers advise that fit points differ in how easily they can be changed: shoulders are the hardest to alter after construction, so tailors usually check shoulder fit first and then adjust length, waist and sleeves. Trouser length conventions vary: Wikipedia says Europeans often choose shorter trousers with little or no break, while Americans often choose a slight break, and that jacket lengths shortened in the mid-2000s to 2010s before returning toward traditional lengths in the 2020s [8]. Fashion changes the target too, with wide trousers in the 1920s, tapering after 1935 and slim lines in the 1980s [8].

There are no medical risks associated with garment alteration. Practical limits are reported by the trade: alteration is constrained by seam allowances and the original construction, and some garments cannot be reshaped satisfactorily. A poorly executed alteration can damage a piece, and the cost relative to the garment price varies [2]. Bespoke work is slow and costly; Wikipedia gives bespoke Italian suits as roughly 1,700 to 3,000 euros and about 40 hours of work [1].

In looksmaxxing and wider men's style discussion, tailoring is typically placed among the inexpensive, low-risk steps for improving presentation, usually described as a way to make a given physique appear more proportionate without surgical or pharmacological intervention. Posters on strength forums mention it in passing; one T Nation poster says his workaround for dress shirts is buying for neck size and using shirt garters because he considers a tailor too costly [9].

No clinical studies found. A 2011 university study of first impressions, run with a tailoring firm, compared made-to-measure and off-the-peg suits on observer ratings of confidence and success; it did not measure attractiveness directly [3].

lore.intro: Fit is a staple of men's style advice, and strength-training forums mention tailoring mostly as a way to make a built or slim frame look proportionate.

claims.claim: Fit matters more than brand or price
claims.believers: Style writers say altering an inexpensive garment can look better than an expensive one that does not fit.
claims.experts: The 2011 Hertfordshire study found a made-to-measure suit rated higher than a similar off-the-peg suit on confidence and success, though it was run with a tailor and not peer reviewed at release [3].

claims.claim: Tailoring makes a physique look more proportionate
claims.believers: Proponents describe shoulders, waist and hems that line up with the body as flattering the wearer's proportions.
claims.experts: No published study located has isolated the effect of alteration on rated attractiveness; the Hertfordshire study rated confidence, success, flexibility and earnings [3].

claims.claim: Bespoke is categorically better than made-to-measure
claims.believers: Savile Row houses and the Savile Row Bespoke Association emphasise individual patterns and many hours of hand labour [5].
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes the lines have blurred, with hand work in made-to-measure and machines in most bespoke, and a 2008 ASA ruling allowed machine-assisted suits to be called bespoke [4][6].

claims.claim: Shirt garters or neck-size buying can substitute for a tailor
claims.believers: A T Nation poster describes this workaround for dress shirts [9].
claims.experts: Tailors describe alteration as limited by seam allowances and original cut [2]; no studies compare the approaches.

claims.claim: Any garment can be tailored to fit
claims.believers: Style advice often treats alteration as a universal fix.
claims.experts: Trade descriptions say alteration is limited by seam allowances and construction, and shoulders are hardest to change [2].

claims.claim: A made-to-measure suit makes the wearer more successful
claims.believers: David Brooke of the tailoring firm Mathieson and Brooke said a made-to-measure suit gives more confidence and ultimately success [3].
claims.experts: The study measured observers' snap judgments, not the wearer's outcomes; the report noted a commercial partner and no peer review at release [3].
